item.title: Earth's 'core carbon' may have come from the far reaches of the solar system
item.description: A new study suggests that most of Earth's carbon originated in the outer solar system and didn't arrive here until the late stages of planetary development. The study, led by researchers at Yale and Columbia, is based upon an analysis of magma droplets called "melt inclusions" from historic volcano eruptions in Hawaii, including the Keanakākoʻi eruptions from 1500 to 1840 and the Kīlauea Iki eruption in 1959.

item.title: How space weather powers auroras in the sky and threatens power grids on the ground
item.description: An aurora is one of nature's most spectacular light shows: It looks like green or red curtains rippling across the night sky. When viewed from the ground, this colorful display might seem far away and disconnected from anything happening on Earth's surface.

item.title: First-of-its-kind planetary wreckage holds clues to our Solar System’s fate
Tiny solar whirlpools may hold the secret to the sun's blistering corona
item.description: For the second time in a few weeks, we're writing about research into the temperature gap between the sun's surface and its corona. More and more data from various missions continue to feed this wave of discovery. A new paper by Katariina Nykyri of Embry-Riddle, recently published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, adds to this growing body of work. She argues that millions of tiny whirlpools scattered across the sun's surface could be the energetic engine driving that temperature difference.

item.title: Taula eclipse
item.description: Josh Dury, taken from Menorca, Spain The Aug. 12, 2026, total solar eclipse sets over Talatí de Dalt, a late Bronze Age settlement on the Spanish island of Menorca. The Sun’s partial phases march down to the horizon, where totality lasted about 73 seconds — the site’s first total eclipse since 1539.
